title: Mahamudra
hookLine: the "great seal": resting in the mind's own nature, taught in the Kagyu school

lines: A KING'S SEAL IN RED WAX.
WHAT IF EVERY THOUGHT CARRIED ONE?
cards: Look at the bottom of an old letter from a king. Pressed into red wax is his seal. It doesn't change the words or add a line, but it marks the whole page: this belongs to the king, this is real.

Now take that picture somewhere stranger. What if every thought, every sound, every mood you've ever had carried a seal like that, a mark showing what it truly is, and you'd simply never looked at the bottom of the page?
The Kagyu school, which you met earlier this year, names its heart practice after that seal. Today: Mahamudra.

teach.b: First, the name. Mahamudra is Sanskrit: maha, great, and mudra, a seal or a sign. The great seal.

Kagyu teachers explain that everything that appears is stamped with the mind's own nature, open and clear. Nothing escapes the seal, so nothing has to be thrown out to find it. Second, the line it comes down.

teach.h: TILOPA TO NAROPA, ON TO GAMPOPA.
teach.b: The Kagyu tell a chain of teachers: the Indian master Tilopa taught Naropa, Naropa taught the Tibetan translator Marpa, Marpa taught Milarepa, and Milarepa taught Gampopa.
Tradition says Tilopa gave Naropa a song of Mahamudra on the banks of the Ganges, comparing the mind to space: space rests on nothing, and nothing stains it.
Other Tibetan schools teach Mahamudra too, but it sits at the heart of the Kagyu. Third, the instruction, which is short.

teach.h: SIX PIECES OF ADVICE, ENDING IN REST.
teach.b: Six pieces of advice attributed to Tilopa are often summed up like this: don't recall the past, don't imagine the future, don't think about now, don't examine, don't control, and rest.
Not to blank the mind, but to stop chasing it. Thoughts still come. They're seen for what they are, marked with the seal, and allowed to go.
Kagyu teachers usually lead students slowly: first steadying the mind, then looking for where a thought comes from and where it goes, and only then resting in what's found.
It's taught by a teacher, step by step, not found in a book in one evening. But the image is simple enough to carry all day: you don't have to remove the thought to find what it's stamped with.

how: In the Kagyu school, students usually receive Mahamudra instruction from a teacher after preliminary practices, training first in calm, then in looking directly at the mind, and finally in resting in its nature; other Tibetan schools also teach Mahamudra.

o: a breathing exercise for calming a busy mind
the great seal: resting in the mind's own nature

games.q: you're sitting in Mahamudra practice and a worry about tomorrow arrives. what does Tilopa's advice say?
o: don't follow it into the future, don't control it: notice, and rest.
games.why: don't recall, don't imagine, don't think, don't examine, don't control, rest: the thought is seen and let go.

practice: Sit upright and easy, eyes open, gaze resting softly a little ahead.
When a thought appears, don't follow it into the past or the future, and don't push it away: notice it, the way you'd notice a seal at the bottom of a page, and let it go.
Then rest in the noticing itself, and if you drift, come back without a fuss.

wordCard.voice: Mahamudra. The great seal: in Kagyu teaching, resting in the mind's own nature, which marks every thought and appearance. Today's word.
